Thousands of households across the north of Scotland have been given emergency battery packs to help see them through winter in what is believed to be a first for an electricity operator in the UK.
Scottish and Southern Electricity Networks (SSEN) Distribution has issued the kit to assist residents during potential power cuts during future storms.

John Swinney has said he opposes a UK government bid to ban new oil and gas exploration in the North Sea, confirming the SNP has U-turned on the issue.
The First Minister said each application should instead be assessed on a case-by-case basis as to whether it is better for the climate than importing fossil fuels.
It comes almost four years after the SNP’S draft energy strategy, published under Nicola Sturgeon, included a presumption against new oil and gas drilling.

URGENT: Save the Glyndŵr National Park & Demand the Promised Public Inquiry (Deadline: Wednesday 11 November)
After four years of evaluation and a 67% to 31% public majority in favour, Natural Resources Wales (NRW) formally concluded that the Clwydian Range, Dee Valley, and Berwyn uplands meet all legal criteria to become Wales's fourth National Park. In March 2026, the Welsh Government promised an independent Public Local Inquiry to examine council objections and local boundary questions.
Now, the Welsh Government has announced it is "minded not to confirm" the National Park and wants to cancel the Public Local Inquiry altogether—giving the public until 11 November 2026 to respond to over 220 pages of newly published, heavily flawed impact assessments.
This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to protect more of Wales’s most treasured landscapes before it is too late. Confirming the National Park will establish a permanent guardian for our extraordinary hills, valleys, deep peatlands, and threatened wildlife—giving conservation the legal priority needed to defend these special places and their surrounding skylines from inappropriate industrial development forever.
We have set up a quick, 3-minute tool that generates a personalised, evidence-based representation demanding that Welsh Ministers confirm the Glyndŵr National Park Designation Order and proceed with the promised Public Local Inquiry.
Submit your representation in 3 minutes here:
https://glyndwr.appeal.direct
(Note: Clicking this link will automatically redirect you to our campaign page hosted on the ObjectNow platform, where your letter is configured in full support of the Glyndŵr National Park and in opposition to cancelling the Public Local Inquiry.)
Please take three minutes to send your letter today and forward this message to friends, family, and neighbours before 11 November!
Shared with thanks by The Dee Valley Environmental Network (DVEN)
OBJECT.NOW Glyndŵr National Park | Campaign

Viking Link Interconnector is a 767km-long, high-voltage direct-current (HVDC) transmission link, built to interconnect the electricity networks of Denmark and the UK. It is one of the world's longest interconnectors.
National Grid Viking Link, a subsidiary of the UK's National Grid; and Energinet, the Danish national transmission system operator (TSO), developed the interconnector project thro a 50:50 joint venture (JV).
The "world's longest” onshore and subsea interconnector was officially been switched on, National Grid confirmed 29th December 2023.
Connecting the UK and Denmark, the £1.7 billion Viking Link will initially operate at a reduced capacity of 800MW due to system constraints put in place by the Danish System Operator, Energinet. This was gradually increased to 1.4GW over 2024.
The link stretches for 475 miles under land and sea to join Bicker Fen substation in Lincolnshire with Revsing substation in southern Jutland, Denmark. It is worth noting that this is National Grid's sixth interconnector and first started development in 2019.
The Viking Link HVDC interconnector operates at a nominal voltage of ±525 kV DC (525,000 volts). Tested up to 735 kV (1.4 times its operational voltage) during pre-commissioning.
Transmission Capacity up to 1,400 MW and Approximately 765 km (475 miles) length 
connecting Bicker Fen in Lincolnshire, UK, with Revsing in South Jutland, Denmark.
National Grid launched the UK's first interconnector (IFA) to France in 1986. Since then, it has built five more including a second link with France (IFA2) and further connections with The Netherlands (BritNed), Belgium (Nemo Link) and Norway (North Sea Link).
Viking Link has a converter station on each end of the cable where the power is transformed into the correct frequency before being transported onto each country's transmission systems. The UK converter station was provided by principal contractor Siemens Energy while Energinet built the Danish converter station.
Siemens Energy designed, installed and commissioned the electrical assets on both sides whilst Prysmian Group manufactured the HVDC land cable which was installed by Balfour Beatty.
Katie Jackson, president of National Grid Ventures, believes that the record-breaking new link will "play a vital role in increasing security of supply and reducing prices for consumers". Jackson also referenced the further influx of green energy used on the Danish grid as another boost to the UK.
It is worth noting that the UK intends to have at least 18GW of interconnection capacity by 2030. Cornwall Insight believes that by the late 2020s, there could be increased exports to the UK's neighbour, France.
France is a key neighbour for importing and exporting energy and, due to issues discovered within France's existing nuclear fleet and its lowest production since 1993, the UK exported vast sums of energy to main the country's energy demands in 2022.— at Denmark.

The new Energy From Waste (EFW) at Shieldhall in Glasgow - the South Clyde Energy Centre, jointly owned by Fortum and Gren.
It's been under construction since late 2022 and looks nearly done, with commercial operations expected by the end of this year.
It'll process up to 350,000 tonnes of residual waste annually which currently goes to landfill. The 35 MW electricity generation produced would be  and enough to power around 70000 homes.
Key Technical Specifications
• Electricity Generation: Up to 45 MWe gross (with a net export of roughly 35 MWe).
• Waste Processing: Up to 350,000 tonnes per year (processing about 44 tonnes per hour).
• Heat Output: 12 MWth of heat (heat-offtake enabled for local businesses or district heating systems).
• Equivalent Power: Enough electricity to power approximately 70,000 homes.
• Location: Land south of King George V Dock in Glasgow, Scotland.
Long term waste contract signed with 5 council areas.— at Shieldhall Waste Disposal & Recycling Centre.

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
Pitlochry or Loch Faskally Hydro power station and dam, along with Clunie dam and power station, constitute the final stage of the Tummel-Garry hydro-electric scheme. Pitlochry has two 7,500kW sets which were both in operation by the end of December 1950. The power station and dam are considered to be, architecturally speaking, one of the most successful of the Hydro-Board's projects. There is no overhead 'clutter' of transformers or power lines as all power is transmitted underground to Clunie power station. The power station is faced in pre-cast concrete to fit in with the mass concrete dam.
Within a few minutes walk from the centre of Pitlochry are the dam and integral generating station. The dam is 54 ft high and the station was designed principally to benefit the lower reaches of the Tummel by evening out the flow of water reaching Clunie power station.
Pitlochry Power Station, Bridge, Dam and Fish Ladder, 1947-50. H O Tarbolton. Ingenious linear amalgamation of power station, bridge and dam across lower end of Loch Faskally, the man-made reservoir. Power station in monumental cubixc style, faced in granite forextra muscularity. Neart nan Gleann (Power of the Glens) reads the Hydro-Electric Board's motto on the N elevation, in case of doubt. 
This group of structures forms a major element of the Tummel/Garry Hydro-electric Scheme. This is the bottom station on the Tummel scheme, and re-uses water that has been previously used to generate power up to 4 times. The station is integrated with the dam in a single structure behind which is created a man made reservoir in Loch Faskally. The dam section has a prominent walkway oversailing tow large drum gates which allow for flood management and control of the spill level. Minimum compensation is provided to the river, with a small compensation set. The turbine hall houses two large turbines. A fish pass is located to the south west end of the dam. 
Pitlochry Dam is one of nine power stations that were constructed in the Tummel Valley hydroelectric scheme. It has two turbines which supply electricity for 15,000 homes
Not all residents however approved of the plan, many concerned that it would decimate the Scottish landscape.
In fact a project encouraged residents to protest and write to their MPs in order to stop the construction of the hydroelectric plants and dams.
Following the uproar the plans were debated in parliament. Despite debates, construction went ahead anyway in 1947 and the first concrete block was laid by the Countess of Airlie.
Care was taken in the dam’s design, ensuring it blended into the landscape as much as possible. More importantly, however, was the incorporation of a fish ladder, enabling migrating fish such as salmon to still be able to travel up and downstream without being hindered by the dam.
The original project was designed by Balfour Beatty and built by Wimpey Construction to a plan approved by the North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board.
Men from across Europe were employed to build the dam and, at its peak, there were around 12,000 men working on the several hydroelectric schemes in the highlands, including ex prisoners of war.
The construction of the Pitlochry dam, completed in 1950, led to the creation of Loch Faskally and the development of sailing, fishing and various forms of water sports making Pitlochry a major tourist centre attracting about 100 000 visitors each year. In the late 1940s and 1950s, when the works were being planned and constructed, Hydro Board staff and their consultant engineers were often ostracised and refused accommodation such was the fear that the works would blight the scenery and drive away visitors.
The two automatic drum gates each with a span of 90ft were the first of their type and size used in Brtain (they were also installed at Clunie Dam) and were designed and built by Glenfield and Kennedy of Kilmarnock. These provide a 'sensitive spill', allowing for very little change in the reservoir levels. The hollow drum gates open automatically, rotating forward on a keel hinge at an angle of travel of 65 degrees into a flotation chamber, thus allowing the impounded water to spill over the crest.
The generating machinery consists of two 7.5MW turbo alternators. Third generator set uses the compensatory water flow to provide some electricity during low water flow periods.
The dam and station at Pitlochry are considered to be one of the most successful architectural designs by NoSHEB. The composition is confident in expressing the cutting edge nature of the industry with a muscular cubic design which is further re-enforced by the granite facing to the turbine hall and the large coat of arms with the legend ‘Power From The Glens’ emblazoned over the main entrance. The design for this building, set within a high profile scenic area and subject to powerful lobbying from influential Perthshire gentry was a test of the power and resolve of the board. The monumental nature of the final design is an expression of the confidence felt by the board at this time. 
The history of electricity supplies across the highlands as recently as 1940s only one in six farms and one in 200 crofts in the highlands had electricity. Politician Tom Johnston set-out a vision for creating a hydroelectric scheme in the Scottish Highlands.
Construction of the dam started in 1947, part of an ambitious scheme to create 78 dams and 54 power stations across the Scottish Highlands
Construction on site was not easy and the 
dam took four years to build, annual flooding at the site leading to delays. As the dam was being built in an existing river it required a system of coffer dams in order to control the spread and flow of water through the site which caused further complications. Adding additional delays to the project was the strike of the workers over poor quality of food. At last construction finished in January 1951 with an opening ceremony planned for June, later that year.
Sadly Sir Edward MacColl, head engineer of the Hydro Board died suddenly just before the opening ceremony. As a result a more sombre ceremony was hosted in 1952 and a plaque in his honour was unveiled at Pitlochry Dam. The dam was then up and running. This was the first time a water storage element had been incorporated into hydropower in Scotland, as opposed to simply relying on the natural flow of rivers to generate power.
Thankfully residents’ initial concerns of a decimated landscape didn’t materialise. In fact, the creation of Loch Faskally atop the dam just added to the area’s beauty and increased tourism. The loch became a popular spot for anglers, kayakers, canoeists, paddleboarders and walkers. The forests surrounding the loch are often used to host the award-winning Enchanted Forest spectacle.
An integral and tourist-friendly part of the Dam is the innovative Fish Ladder. Because thousands of Atlantic salmon and other fish return to the place where they were spawned in order to lay fresh eggs, a way had to be developed to allow them to bypass the dam and follow the river Tummel upstream to spawn.
The fish ladder (along with the more extensive one at Clunie power station and dam) is of the 'pool and orifice' type. The innovative solution built into the design of the dam is a 310 metre long Fish Ladder, which allows the fish to pass through the dam en route to their spawning area. There is a visitor path which climbs alongside the ladder, allowing you the opportunity to search the pools for an elusive salmon.
There is a celebration each January to announce the start of the salmon season. Many salmon start swimming through the ladder in spring with the peak being between April and the end of August. The late salmon run starts in September and ends in October.
The Fish Ladder has 34 chambers (including 3 resting chambers to give the fish time to rest during their ascent) which are essentially small, artificial pools, each one with a water level slightly higher than the one below which, in turn, creates a series of steps for the fish to tackle, slowly taking the fish up to Loch Faskally.
The fish swim from one chamber to the next via small circular entrances beneath each wooden entrance to the chambers. These entrances restrict the amount of water flowing from one chamber to the next and a continuous flow of water via these entrances maintains the water level in the Fish Ladder.
The dam’s award-winning visitor centre was opened in 2017, stationed with a glorious panoramic view of the dam.— in Pitlochry.

Forth Ports Leith Docks
Screening opinion sought by Forth Ports & Nova Innovation for a floating photovoltaic (FPV) array in Victoria Dock - Nova Innovation have been running a demonstrator project nearby for the last few years. A similar project for this site was first mooted over a decade ago.
The Proposed Development is anticipated to consist of a floating Solar Photovoltaic Array with a capacity in the region of 0.5MW with a private wire cable connecting the Solar array to a new substation located c. 40m to the north. This connection would comprise an underwater array cable which would run underneath the bridge on Ocean Drive.
We understand that water levels in the docks are maintained by Forth Ports by lock gates/sealing infrastructure. Water levels can change within parameters but are normally maintained around 2.6- 2.8m AOD. The water level is therefore not generally affected by the tides, and the height of the solar array as it sits in the Dock will not substantially change during its operational lifespan.
The floating solar array would be anchored to concrete ballast blocks via mooring lines which will then be lowered to sit on the seabed using gravity. The array will not be connected to the dock wall or any other part of the dock. The top of the solar panels will sit around 0.9m from the surface of the water once installed, angled at 11 degrees. These will be mounted on a plastic subframe, attached in turn to the array floats. 
The array shall be assembled on the north-east quayside of the Albert Dock Basin, within the Forth Ports operational area. Floating modules will be lifted into the water and towed into Victoria Dock under the bridge of Ocean Drive. Deployment will take approximately 3 weeks, including deployment of the ballast blocks and final electrical connections on the array.
The proposed substation will be located on vacant land to the north. It will have a floor area of 20sqm and will be approximately 2.5m in height. The material finish is proposed to be green glass- reinforced plastic The substation will be constructed on site in four main stages:
Groundworks - the area underneath the substation will be excavated to expose firm ground upon which the substation can be built. This shall also accommodate an electrical earthing grid and include exposing the existing HV power cable which the substation will connect to.
Foundation installation - the formwork and rebar for the foundation shall be put in place, with concrete poured on site.
Transformer and GRP housing installation - the transformer will be placed onto the concrete foundation and the GRP housing erected over the top of this.
Electrical connection - the electrical connections to the HV cable and floating solar array will be made and energised following grid operator witnessing.
Works shall be completed in accordance with Edinburgh Tram's Authority to Work (ATW) Permit procedure. This will likely include periodic isolation of the relevant section of the tram network during night-time hours.
Temporary perimeter fencing (e.g. Heras fencing) will be used around the proposed substation during the construction phase and is planned to be removed following completion of construction. No CCTV is currently planned for the array. The substation will be padlocked to prohibit access during its operational life.
The Proposed Development has no fixed operational lifespan, the array is intended to operate for a long-term period, and its lifespan prolonged through ongoing maintenance, component replacement and repowering carried out by Forth Ports.
The purpose of the Proposed Development is to generate clean and renewable energy to support Forth Dorts in the day-to-day operation— at Leith Docks.

UK Power Networks sent a 47-strong team to Scotland last week, to help restore power to people without electricity after Storm Boelo.
Responding to a callout for volunteer support from SSEN, the team set off Monday and reported for duty Tuesday. This process that's available to all DNOs during major incidents.
Collaborating with local teams, this skilled contingent worked in challenging conditions to help reconnect power for thousands of customers. Some teams found themselves further afield, with a Risby-based team working on the island of Colonsay to restore supplies to all 120 residents.— in Scotland.

records.bodyText: Whilst I was doing some research into substation upgrades I decided to take another look at the Mossmorran BESS and discovered the developer had held an online community consultation on Monday 2nd November 2026. Apparently Gresham House is applying for an amendment to the original scheme that was previously granted planning permission by the Energy Consents Unit. I am keeping a watch on this development as ILI appear to have an agreed connection to the Mossmorran BESS. I checked where the event had been advertised as nobody seemed to be aware of it, including Auchtertool Community Council. It appears the event was advertised via something called the Public Notice Portal. A platform that has about 7% public usage. I’m pretty sure only advertising on this platform is in breach of the statutory legal requirements. I have watched the recording of the event and I am fairly sure there was no one attending the event; there were no questions and answers which seemed odd. I have submitted some questions to Gresham House via their feedback email and I’m awaiting a response.
